Cardiology and hematology · published research

Angiogenesis (promotion of)

Some cell and animal studies report increases in vessel formation, perfusion, or endothelial activity, while other results are null or depend on the model and protocol. No human trial has tested PBM specifically to promote angiogenesis.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Selected laboratory and animal experiments report angiogenesis-related changes, including altered endothelial migration, tube formation, vessel density, or perfusion. Findings vary across models and light protocols, and they do not establish a clinical benefit in people.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM has produced angiogenesis-related responses in some cell and animal models, but not consistently across protocols. Several studies combine light with stem-cell or biomaterial approaches, and their results do not show that PBM alone would produce the same effect. No human clinical study tests PBM specifically to promote angiogenesis.

Human and clinical evidence

No patient treatment trial was identified for PBM used specifically to promote angiogenesis. Experiments using human endothelial cells are laboratory studies, not clinical treatment evidence.

Animal evidence

Animal experiments use rat, mouse, rabbit, and chick-embryo models to examine wound healing, limb ischemia, collateral growth, or tissue repair. A rat ischemic-flap experiment reported increased vessel formation and perfusion with LED treatment, alongside less tissue necrosis (Dungel et al. 2014).

Other studies report increased collateral growth or blood-flow recovery in mouse and rabbit ischemia models. A 2024 rat lower-limb ischemia experiment found several vascular and tissue measures comparable with its control group, illustrating that findings are not uniform (Perez et al. 2024).

A 2025 mouse hindlimb-ischemia study reported improved blood-flow recovery at 14 days after daily 652-nm PBM, with little effect at day 5 (Joniová et al. 2025). A separate rat study tested PBM with bioactive glass; the combination arm cannot isolate the independent contribution of light (Huang et al. 2022).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell experiments report changes in endothelial-cell viability, migration, proliferation, and tube formation. In one wound-healing study, 633-nm PBM at 1.0 J/cm² affected these outcomes and was linked to VEGFR2 and STAT3 signaling (Zhang et al. 2022). A 635-nm pulsed LED study reported angiogenesis-related responses in cell culture and a chick-embryo membrane model (Winter et al. 2018).

The 2025 mouse study also included ex-vivo aortic rings and a chick-embryo membrane assay (Joniová et al. 2025).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The studies use different light sources and settings rather than a shared protocol. Tested wavelengths include blue and red visible light and near-infrared light. Examples include 633 nm at 1.0 J/cm² in the Zhang study, 635-nm pulsed LED in the Winter study, and daily 652-nm treatment in the 2025 mouse experiment (Zhang et al. 2022; Winter et al. 2018; Joniová et al. 2025). Power, fluence, exposure time, schedule, tissue target, and co-interventions also vary. The available findings do not establish an optimal dose or show that experimental vessel growth leads to durable, functional circulation in people.

Interpretation

Some experiments show changes in angiogenesis markers or perfusion, while other findings are smaller or null. The evidence supports context-specific biological responses in laboratory and animal models, not a general clinical effect. Studies in people would need to test a defined condition and measure functional outcomes.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for a general angiogenesis or vascular-function benefit in people. The evidence is preclinical, uses varied models and protocols, and includes mixed results.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The evidence consists of laboratory and animal studies with varied wavelengths, doses, models, and outcomes. Some studies report favorable changes in vessel formation or perfusion, while others are null or context-dependent. Combinations with stem cells or biomaterials complicate attribution to light alone, and no patient outcomes have been tested. A defined clinical condition, standardized dose reporting, and functional outcomes would be needed to support a stronger conclusion (Dungel et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2022; Joniová et al. 2025).
